title: ferroplan-sat: the SAT solver
summary: The in-tree CDCL SAT solver behind the SAT compilation wing: how it searches, how it stores clauses, and how the planner drives it.
body: This section covers crates/ferroplan-sat. Start with the CDCL main loop for the algorithm in five steps, then open the modules for the data structures that make each step fast. The planner-side encoding lives in mod-sat; this section only describes how that encoding calls the solver.

children.title: ferroplan-sat crate
children.summary: A ~5k-line, zero-dependency CDCL SAT solver absorbed from varisat 0.2.2: watched literals, 1UIP learning, VSIDS, Luby restarts, tiered clause DB, assumptions, conflict budget.
children.body:
A SAT solver decides whether a propositional formula in conjunctive normal form has a satisfying assignment, and produces one if so. ferroplan-sat is a textbook-modern CDCL solver: two-watched-literal propagation with blocking literals, first-UIP conflict analysis with recursive minimization, VSIDS branching with phase saving, Luby restarts, a glue-tiered learned-clause database with activity-based reduction and copying GC, and an incremental assumptions interface. It is MiniSat/Glucose-class in design, without preprocessing (no variable elimination, no inprocessing beyond level-0 simplification).

Layering: Solver (public) wraps Context (all state); schedule_step drives conflict_step; propagation, analysis, decision and clause storage are separate modules that take &mut Context and destructure the fields they need.

It exists to serve the planner's SAT compilation wing, but has no planning-specific dependencies.

children.title: CDCL main loop
children.summary: decide, propagate, analyze, learn/backjump, restart: the five-beat loop driven by schedule_step and conflict_step.
children.body:
CDCL (conflict-driven clause learning) is the algorithm behind every modern SAT solver. A formula in CNF is a conjunction of clauses, each clause a disjunction of literals. The solver builds a partial assignment by guessing a variable (a decision), then deducing everything that guess forces (unit propagation). When the deductions contradict a clause, it analyses why, learns a new clause that rules out that whole family of mistakes, jumps back to the earliest decision where the new clause forces something, and continues. Periodically it restarts from scratch while keeping what it learned.

In ferroplan-sat the outer driver is schedule_step (one call per conflict: maybe restart, maybe reduce the clause database, maybe garbage-collect, then conflict_step). conflict_step runs find_conflict, a loop of propagate, settle units, enqueue the next assumption, decide; when it reports a conflict, conflict_step analyses it, bumps involved clauses, backtracks, stores the learned clause and enqueues its asserting literal.

children.title: 1. Decide
children.summary: Pick the unassigned variable with the highest VSIDS activity, give it its saved phase, and open a new decision level.
children.body:
When propagation has nothing more to deduce and all assumptions are placed, make_decision pops variables off the VSIDS max-heap (vsids.find(...) uses the heap's Iterator impl) until it finds one that is still unassigned. Popped-but-assigned variables are simply dropped from the heap; backtrack puts them back when they become unassigned again.

The polarity is the variable's saved phase: assignment.last_var_value(var), the value it held the last time it was unassigned by backtracking. A never-assigned variable defaults to false, which for planning CNFs means "no op at this layer" - the 0.25 record calls this sparse-plan polarity free.

The decision then calls trail.new_decision_level() and enqueues the literal with Reason::Unit (decisions have no reason clause). If no unassigned variable remains, make_decision returns false and find_conflict reports a full satisfying assignment, which reconstruct_global_model turns into the model.

children.title: 2. Propagate (BCP)
children.summary: Drain the trail queue: for each newly true literal, fire binary implications, then scan long-clause watch lists for clauses that became unit or false.
children.body:
Boolean constraint propagation: if all but one literal of a clause are false, the last one must be true. prop::propagate pops literals from the trail's queue and, for each, calls propagate_binary (direct implication lists, cheapest) and then propagate_long (two-watched-literal scan). Every forced literal is enqueued with its Reason and goes onto the same queue, so propagation runs to fixpoint.

The first clause found with all literals false is returned as a Conflict (Binary([a,b]) or Long(cref)). Before acting on it, find_conflict calls prove_units: if the solver is at level 0, everything on the trail is a permanent fact and is moved off the trail. If new units appeared and there was no conflict, unit_simplify cleans the clause database.

Propagation dominates solver run time, which is why prop/long.rs keeps upstream's raw-pointer watch-list scan verbatim.

children.title: 3. Analyze conflict (1UIP)
children.summary: Resolve the conflicting clause backwards along the trail until exactly one literal of the current level remains: the first unique implication point.
children.body:
The conflict says: these literals cannot all be false together. Some of them were forced at the current decision level. analyze_conflict walks the trail backwards and repeatedly replaces a current-level literal with the reason clause that forced it (a resolution step), stopping as soon as only one current-level literal remains. That literal is the first UIP; its negation becomes position 0 of the learned clause, which will assert it after backjumping.

Along the way every variable touched is VSIDS-bumped, and every long clause used is recorded in involved for clause-activity bumping. The clause is then shortened by recursive minimization. Finally the literal with the highest remaining decision level is swapped into position 1 (needed for the watch invariant) and its level is returned as the backjump target. A conflict at level 0 produces the empty clause: the formula is UNSAT.

children.title: 4. Learn and backjump
children.summary: Bump involved clauses, backtrack to the asserting level, store the learned clause by size, and enqueue its first literal.
children.body:
Back in conflict_step: each clause in analyze.involved() goes through bump_clause (activity bump, glue recomputation, possible tier promotion), clause activities decay, and backtrack(ctx, backtrack_to) undoes every level above the target. This is non-chronological backtracking: the solver may skip many decision levels at once, because the learned clause proves none of them mattered.

Storage depends on the learned clause length:

  • 0 literals: SatState::Unsat.
  • 1 literal: a new unit, enqueued with Reason::Unit (at level 0).
  • 2 literals: added to BinaryClauses, reason Reason::Binary.
  • 3+: assess_learned_clause computes glue and tier, db::add_clause stores and watches it, reason Reason::Long(cref).

Then enqueue_assignment puts clause[0] on the trail. The next propagate round continues from there.

children.title: 5. Restart and housekeeping
children.summary: Between conflicts, schedule_step restarts on a Luby schedule, halves or demotes learned clauses, collects garbage, and enforces the conflict budget.
children.body:
A restart undoes all decisions (but keeps assumptions, learned clauses, activities and saved phases). It lets the solver escape a bad early decision that conflict analysis cannot reach. schedule_step restarts when the conflict count hits next_restart, then advances next_restart by 128 * luby.advance() conflicts.

On the same per-conflict tick it runs reduce_locals every 15,000 conflicts and reduce_mids every 10,000 (both at conflict 0 too, harmlessly), and collect_garbage whenever deleted clauses exceed half of the clause arena.

Before any of that it checks conflict_limit: if this solve call has spent its budget, it stops with the state left honestly Unknown, which Solver::solve reports as Err(SolverError::Interrupted). The loop then returns to step 1.

children.title: Public API
children.summary: What a caller sees: Solver, its incremental methods, the conflict budget, assumptions, model, and the seeding hook.
children.body: The crate exports four modules (cnf, dimacs, lit, solver); everything else is private. This group covers the caller-facing behaviours; the internals below implement them.

children.title: Solver: the public facade
children.summary: Solver wraps a boxed Context and exposes add_clause/new_var, solve, model, assume, failed_core, set_conflict_limit and seed_activity.
children.body:
Solver is the whole public surface (re-exported from lib.rs with Lit, Var, CnfFormula, ExtendFormula). It holds a Box<Context>.

  • add_clause / add_formula go through load_clause; new_var allocates a user variable (via the ExtendFormula trait, shared with CnfFormula).
  • solve() resets conflicts_this_solve, loops while schedule_step(ctx) {}, and maps SatState: Sat to Ok(true), Unsat/UnsatUnderAssumptions to Ok(false), Unknown to Err(Interrupted).
  • model() returns user-variable literals when SAT.
  • assume(&[Lit]) and failed_core(): incremental assumptions.
  • set_conflict_limit(Option<u64>): the ferroplan addition.
  • seed_activity(&[(usize, f32)]): the planning-branching hook.

The solver is incremental: adding a clause after SAT flips the state back to Unknown and does a full_restart; adding to an UNSAT solver is a no-op. SolverError is #[non_exhaustive] with one variant, Interrupted, which is recoverable.

children.title: Conflict budget (Interrupted)
children.summary: The one feature ferroplan added during absorption: a per-solve conflict cap that stops with an honest third verdict and can be resumed.
children.body:
A SAT solver on a hard instance can run indefinitely. The planner's horizon ramp needs to say "no answer within this many conflicts" without claiming UNSAT. Schedule carries conflict_limit: Option<u64> and conflicts_this_solve; schedule_step returns false once the count reaches the limit, leaving sat_state == Unknown.

The interrupt is recoverable: nothing is torn down, so raising or clearing the limit and calling solve again continues with all learned clauses intact. satdiff_conflict_budget_interrupts pins this: a limit of 5 interrupts a pigeonhole instance, then None lets it finish UNSAT.

The planner uses it in slices: solve_horizon sets set_conflict_limit(Some(slice)) with SLICE = 4_096, accumulates spent conflicts against the per-horizon budget, and between slices can bail early if the measured conflict rate says the budget cannot finish in the remaining wall-clock slice. A budget trip is reported as "no plan within horizon H", never as unsolvable.

children.title: Assumptions and failed cores
children.summary: Temporary unit literals placed as the first decision levels; if they clash, a backward trail walk reports which assumptions are to blame.
children.body:
Assumptions let a caller ask "is the formula SAT if these literals are also true?" without adding permanent clauses, so learned clauses stay valid across calls. set_assumptions does a full_restart, maps user to solver literals, and flags each variable assumed (so unit_simplify will not recycle it).

During search, enqueue_assumption treats assumption i as decision level i+1: if it is unassigned it opens a level and enqueues it; if it is already true (implied by earlier ones) it is swap_removed; if it is already false, analyze_assumption_conflict walks the trail backwards from it, following reasons, and collects every level->0 Reason::Unit literal it reaches (these are exactly earlier assumptions). That set is the failed core, not guaranteed minimal. restart only backtracks to assumption_levels, so assumptions survive restarts.

Kept after the strip audit (~200 lines, no dependencies) because the temporal CEGAR loop might want cores. The current planner wing re-encodes each horizon into a fresh solver and does not call assume.

children.title: Model extraction
children.summary: On SAT, copy solver-variable values back to global variables, filling recycled units from VarData, then translate to user literals.
children.body:
When find_conflict finds no variable left to decide, reconstruct_global_model builds Model::assignment indexed by global variable: for each live global var, if it still has a solver var its value is read from the current assignment; otherwise the variable was simplified away and its value comes from VarData::unit, defaulting to false for isolated variables that never mattered. Then it sets SatState::Sat.

Solver::model() maps each user variable through global_from_user and emits user_var.lit(value). Because the user-to-global mapping is the identity in ferroplan's stripped version, the model's literal indices equal the planner's own variable numbering. The planner's decoder reads "unassigned" as false.

children.title: seed_activity: the branching hook
children.summary: Lets the encoder pre-raise VSIDS activity of chosen variables. The reason the solver was absorbed; measured, and left opt-in.
children.body:
Solver::seed_activity takes (user variable index, activity) pairs, translates each to a global variable (exactly as model does) and calls Vsids::seed, which only ever raises an activity and sifts the variable up the heap. Early decisions then follow the caller's structural prior; as real conflict bumps grow (the bump value grows geometrically) the seed washes out.

0.25 Wing II step 5 measured it. Forward layer-ordered op seeding (FF_SAT_BRANCH=fwd: op variables at earlier layers get higher activity) gave a real 1.8x on deep UNSAT proofs (storage-t h1-32: 6.8 s to 3.7 s) but was disqualifying on the SAT side: TMS-2011 i2 at h16 went from one STN refutation and 0.6 s to 247 refutations and a capped budget, because early-packed models are the schedule-infeasible ones. back was 2x worse, uniform worse on both. So the hook ships opt-in, default off (stock heap order); CEGAR-aware seeding is the named 0.26 residue.

children.title: Literals, formulas, variables
children.summary: The vocabulary types and the central Context.
children.body: Everything else in the crate operates on these: compact literals, the flat CNF container, the three-level variable mapping, and the single Context struct that owns all state.

children.title: Literals and variables
children.summary: Var is a u32 index; Lit packs index and sign as code = 2*index + negated, so negation is XOR 1 and literals index arrays directly.
children.body:
A variable is a boolean unknown; a literal is a variable or its negation. Var wraps a 0-based u32 (LitIdx). Lit stores a single code: (index << 1) | negated. So !lit is code ^ 1, lit.var() is code >> 1, and per-literal tables (watch lists, binary implication lists, TmpFlags) are plain Vecs of length 2 * var_count indexed by lit.code().

Var::max_var() is u32::MAX >> 4, leaving spare bits for tags and sentinels. User I/O uses the DIMACS convention: 1-based, sign gives polarity (Lit::from_dimacs(-3) is NOT x3); Debug/Display print that form. Lit ^ bool conditionally negates. Both types are #[repr(transparent)], which lets the clause arena reinterpret a [u32] slice as [Lit].

The planner constructs literals with Lit::from_index(v, true/false) over its own variable numbering.

children.title: CnfFormula
children.summary: A flat formula container: one literal buffer plus a Vec of ranges, implementing ExtendFormula like the solver does.
children.body:
CnfFormula is equivalent to Vec<Vec<Lit>> but stores all literals in one Vec<Lit> with a Vec<Range<usize>> of clause boundaries, avoiding one allocation per clause. var_count tracks the highest variable seen (plus any explicit set_var_count, used to honour a DIMACS header).

The ExtendFormula trait (add_clause, new_var, default new_lit) is implemented both by CnfFormula and by Solver, so code that builds clauses can target either a stored formula or a live solver. Solver::add_formula streams a CnfFormula into the solver. It is what parse_dimacs produces and what the satdiff battery checks models against.

children.title: Variables
children.summary: Variable namespaces and metadata (variables.rs, variables/).
children.body: The variable layer translates caller literals into internal ones on every clause and assumption load (solver_from_user_lits) and back again for models and failed cores (existing_user_from_solver).

children.title: User / global / solver mapping
children.summary: Three variable namespaces: user (caller's numbering), global (identity here), solver (dense internal slots that get recycled).
children.body:
The solver keeps two bidirectional maps (VarBiMap, each a forward and backward VarMap with a watermark). User variables are what the caller names. Global variables are stable identities with metadata; in ferroplan's stripped version the user-to-global map is always the identity because nothing hides user variables. Solver variables are the dense indices all internal arrays use.

Solver variables are allocated lazily: solver_from_global picks a slot from solver_freelist or the next index, grows every per-variable structure via context::set_var_count, and runs initialize_solver_var (restore a known unit value, reset VSIDS activity, put it in the heap if unassigned). When unit_simplify finds a variable fixed or isolated, remove_solver_var takes it off the heap and returns its slot to the freelist; the global variable and its remembered unit value stay. This is why the mapping layer survived the strip: it is a real memory and speed feature, not proof residue.

children.title: VarData flags
children.summary: Per-global-variable metadata: remembered unit value, isolated, assumed, deleted.
children.body:
VarData lives per global variable, so it survives the solver slot being recycled.

  • unit: Option<bool> - the value fixed by a unit clause, remembered after the variable leaves the solver; used by model reconstruction and by initialize_solver_var if the variable is re-mapped.
  • isolated - true while no clause links this variable to another (only unit clauses or none). load_clause clears it for every literal of a clause of length 2+.
  • assumed - part of the current assumptions; protects it from removal.
  • deleted - default true for unallocated slots; user_default() sets it false.

unit_simplify uses these to decide removal: any assigned variable becomes unit = Some(v), isolated = true, and is removed unless assumed.

children.title: Context, config, scratch
children.summary: One plain struct holding every solver part; SolverConfig defaults; TmpData/TmpFlags scratch buffers.
children.body:
Context has one field per subsystem: analyze_conflict, assignment, assumptions, binary_clauses, clause_activity, clause_alloc, clause_db, impl_graph, model, schedule, solver_config, solver_state, tmp_data, tmp_flags, trail, variables, vsids, watchlists. Upstream used the partial_ref macro crate to hand each function a typed view of just the fields it needed. The absorption replaced that with &mut Context plus explicit field destructuring (let Context { assignment, trail, .. } = ctx;), and where a part must be held across a whole-context call it is mem::taken out and put back (for example the watch lists and clause arena during propagate_long). set_var_count fans a new variable count out to every per-variable array.

SolverConfig is a plain struct: vsids_decay 0.95, clause_activity_decay 0.999, reduce_locals_interval 15,000, reduce_mids_interval 10,000, luby_restart_interval_scale 128. Only the intervals and Luby scale are read from the context; both decays are read from SolverConfig::default() when Vsids/ClauseActivity are constructed. There is no public setter.

TmpData holds two reusable literal buffers for load_clause; TmpFlags is a per-literal bool array kept all-false between uses (glue computation, failed-core walk).

children.title: Propagation (prop/)
children.summary: Unit propagation: assignment and trail, implication graph, binary implication lists, two-watched-literal long-clause scan.
children.body: prop.rs is 35 lines: enable watch lists, then for each literal popped from the trail queue run binary then long propagation, returning the first conflict. The submodules hold the state that propagation reads and writes.

children.title: Assignment and trail
children.summary: Per-variable Option<bool> plus saved phase; the trail is the ordered stack of assigned literals with decision-level boundaries and a propagation queue head.
children.body:
Assignment holds Vec<Option<bool>> and last_value (phase saving). lit_is_true/false/unk compare the option as a raw byte via fast_option_eq, a codegen workaround on the hottest path.

Trail is a Vec<Lit> in assignment order, a queue_head_pos (everything after it is assigned but not yet propagated, so the trail doubles as the BCP queue), and decisions, the trail index where each level begins. current_level() is decisions.len().

enqueue_assignment is the single funnel for every assignment (decision, propagation, unit, assumption): set the value, push to trail, record reason, level and trail depth in the implication graph. backtrack(level) truncates the trail to that level's start, unassigns each popped variable, saves its value in last_value, and calls vsids.make_available. Watch lists need no update on backtrack. restart backtracks to the assumption levels; full_restart to 0.

children.title: Implication graph and reasons
children.summary: For each assigned variable: why (Unit, Binary, or Long clause), at what level, at what trail depth. Conflict analysis walks it backwards.
children.body:
The implication graph is a DAG: sources are decisions, assumptions and unit clauses; every propagated literal has edges from the literals that forced it. It is stored implicitly, one ImplNode { reason, level, depth } per variable.

Reason is Unit (no antecedent), Binary([lit]) (the other literal of a binary clause, already negated so it is the false literal), or Long(ClauseRef). For long clauses the propagated literal is always kept at position 0, so reason.lits(alloc) is just clause.lits()[1..] with no copy. Conflict is Binary([a,b]) or Long(cref).

A depth of LitIdx::MAX marks a removed unit: a level-0 fact that prove_units moved off the trail. Garbage collection rewrites Long reasons when clauses move (update_reason).

children.title: Binary clauses
children.summary: Two-literal clauses are not stored as clauses at all: each (a or b) becomes two implication-list entries, !a implies b and !b implies a.
children.body:
Binary clauses are very common in planning encodings (precondition clauses op => pre, mutexes, frame pieces) and propagate in the simplest possible way. BinaryClauses::add_binary_clause([a, b]) pushes b onto the list for !a and a onto the list for !b; implied(lit) returns that slice.

propagate_binary walks the list for the literal just made true: an implied literal that is already false is a conflict Conflict::Binary([implied, !lit]); an unassigned one is enqueued with Reason::Binary([!lit]). No watch lists, no clause arena access. It runs before the long-clause scan for each trail literal.

simplify_binary (called by unit_simplify) drops every list for an assigned literal and every entry mentioning an assigned literal, then recounts. Long clauses shortened to two literals by simplification migrate here too.

children.title: Two watched literals
children.summary: Each long clause is watched by two of its literals; it only needs inspecting when one of those becomes false. Blocking literals skip even that.
children.body:
The naive way to detect that a clause became unit is to recount its false literals on every assignment. The two-watched-literal scheme instead keeps, for every clause of length 3+, two watches in positions 0 and 1. Invariant: if the clause is not unit, both watched literals are non-false. A clause can only become unit or conflicting when a watched literal goes false, so only those clauses are touched. Unassigning never breaks the invariant, so backtracking costs nothing here.

Each Watch { cref, blocking } lives in the list of the literal whose truth triggers it (watch_clause adds to !lits[i]). blocking is some other literal of the clause; if it is already true the clause is satisfied and the scan moves on without touching clause memory (MiniSat 2.1 blocking literals, Sorensson and Een).

Watch lists can be disabled (disable()) when clauses are deleted or moved; enable_watchlists, called at the top of every propagate, then rebuilds all of them from the clause database. Upstream left a TODO in delete_clause about avoiding this full rebuild.

children.title: Long-clause watch scan
children.summary: The hot loop: for each watch of a false literal, keep it, move it to a new non-false literal, propagate the other watch, or report conflict.
children.body:
propagate_long(lit) takes the watch lists and clause arena out of the context and runs scan_watchlist, an unsafe raw-pointer compaction loop kept verbatim from upstream (it still performs bound checks through check_bounds). For each watch in the list for lit:

  1. Blocking literal true: keep the watch, next.
  2. Ensure the now-false literal is at position 1 (swap with 0 if needed). Make a new watch with the other watched literal as blocker.
  3. If that other watched literal is true: keep, next.
  4. Search positions 2.. for a non-false literal. If found, swap it into position 1 and add the watch to its list (this watch leaves the current list).
  5. None found: keep the watch. If position 0 is false, copy the remaining watches, truncate, return Conflict::Long(cref). Otherwise enqueue position 0 with Reason::Long(cref).

The read/write pointer pair compacts the list in place as watches move away, then truncates once at the end.

children.title: Clause storage (clause/)
children.summary: Binary clauses as implication lists, long clauses in a bump arena with packed headers, tiered by glue, reduced by activity, compacted by GC.
children.body: Clauses are stored by size: units never become clauses (they are trail assignments, then VarData::unit), binaries are implication lists (see Propagation), and clauses of 3+ literals go through clause/. The submodules below cover the arena, header, database tiers, quality measures and the two cleanup mechanisms.

children.title: Clause arena (ClauseAlloc)
children.summary: All long clauses live in one Vec<u32> bump arena; a ClauseRef is a 32-bit offset; deleted clauses are reclaimed only by copying GC.
children.body:
ClauseAlloc is a single Vec<LitIdx>. add_clause appends the 3-word header and then the literals (reinterpreted as u32, legal because Lit is repr(transparent)) and returns ClauseRef { offset: u32 }. Offsets stay valid when the Vec grows. Clauses of fewer than 3 literals are refused by assertion: units go on the trail, binaries to BinaryClauses, which lets the propagation loop read positions 0-2 after one bound check.

Clause is a #[repr(transparent)] wrapper around [LitIdx] (header plus literals) with unsafe casts for header() and lits(); upstream notes a proper DST struct is almost impossible to use in stable Rust. Individual clauses are never freed; space returns only through collect_garbage.

Benefits: cache locality during the watch scan, 4-byte clause references in every watch and reason, and no per-clause allocation.

children.title: Clause header bit layout
children.summary: Three u32 words before each clause: activity (f32 bits), a packed word of tier/deleted/mark/glue/active, and length.
children.body:
ClauseHeader is [LitIdx; 3]:

WordBitsField
0allactivity (f32 via to_bits)
10-1tier (Irred, Core, Mid, Local)
12deleted
13mark (temporary; must be reset)
14-9glue (6 bits, saturates at 63)
110active (used in a conflict since last mid reduction)
2alllen

mark is reused by two routines: dedup_and_mark_by_tier uses it to drop duplicate tier-list entries, and GC uses it to flag clauses that are currently a propagation reason. A round-trip test pins the layout.

children.title: Clause database and tiers
children.summary: ClauseDb indexes long clauses by tier (Irred, Core, Mid, Local) with lazy deletion and exact per-tier counts.
children.body:
Learned clauses are useful but unbounded; keeping all of them slows propagation. Following Chanseok Oh ("Between SAT and UNSAT", 2015, section 4), long clauses are partitioned into four Tiers:

  • Irred: original problem clauses, never deleted by reduction.
  • Core: learned with glue <= 2, kept forever.
  • Mid: glue 3-6, kept while recently active.
  • Local: glue >= 7 or demoted, half deleted periodically.

ClauseDb holds clauses (all refs), by_tier lists, count_by_tier (always exact) and garbage_size. Removal is lazy: by_tier may contain deleted, moved, or duplicate refs, and readers check the header. add_clause stores, watches positions 0 and 1, and indexes. set_clause_tier moves a clause by pushing it to the new list. delete_clause sets the header bit, adjusts counts and garbage, and disables watch lists. try_delete_clause refuses to delete a clause that is currently the reason for its literal 0. filter_clauses is the bulk-filter used by unit simplification.

children.title: Glue (LBD) and assessment
children.summary: Glue = number of distinct decision levels in a clause. Low glue predicts a useful learned clause; it picks the tier and can only improve.
children.body:
Literal block distance (LBD, from the Glucose solver) counts how many different decision levels a clause's literals were assigned at. A clause with glue 2 links just two decision "blocks" and tends to propagate again and again; high-glue clauses are usually one-offs. compute_glue marks each literal's level in TmpFlags, counts first marks, then clears them.

assess_learned_clause computes glue while the clause is still in conflict and subtracts 1 (after backjump the asserting literal moves to a new level), then select_tier: glue <= 2 Core, <= 6 Mid, else Local.

bump_clause, called for each long clause used in conflict analysis, bumps clause activity, sets active, recomputes glue under the current assignment, and if it is lower than the stored glue, stores it and promotes the clause's tier. Glue therefore records the best value ever observed.

children.title: Clause activity
children.summary: A VSIDS-style score per clause, bumped when it participates in a conflict and decayed by 0.999 per conflict; ranks Local clauses for deletion.
children.body:
Each long clause's header stores an f32 activity. bump_clause_activity adds the current bump; decay_clause_activities (once per conflict in conflict_step) multiplies bump by 1/0.999 instead of shrinking every clause. The effect is identical up to a common scale factor, and only relative order matters. When bump or any activity exceeds f32::MAX / 16, rescale_clause_activities multiplies every live clause's activity and the bump by the inverse (and prunes deleted refs from clauses on the way).

Activity is only consulted by reduce_locals: it sorts Local clauses by activity (ties by ref) and deletes the least active half.

children.title: Clause DB reduction
children.summary: Every 15k conflicts delete the less active half of Local clauses; every 10k conflicts demote Mid clauses that were not active to Local.
children.body:
Two periodic passes, both triggered from schedule_step by conflict count modulo the config interval:

  • reduce_locals (every 15,000): dedup the Local list (using the header mark), sort by activity ascending, and try to delete the first half. try_delete_clause skips any clause currently acting as a reason, so a few low-activity clauses can survive.
  • reduce_mids (every 10,000): for each Mid clause, if its active bit is set, clear it and keep; otherwise move it to Local, where it competes for survival in the next local reduction.

Core and Irred clauses are never touched. The result is a three-speed memory: a permanent core of low-glue clauses, a middle band kept while useful, and a churning local pool. Deletion only flags headers; memory is reclaimed by GC.

children.title: Garbage collection
children.summary: When deleted clauses exceed half the arena, copy live clauses into a fresh arena (2x headroom) and patch every reason reference.
children.body:
collect_garbage runs each schedule step but only acts when garbage_size * 2 > buffer_size, amortising copy cost. collect_garbage_now:

  1. Disables watch lists (they hold old refs; they are rebuilt at the next propagate).
  2. mark_asserting_clauses: sets the mark bit on every clause that is the Reason::Long of a trail literal.
  3. Allocates a new arena with capacity twice the live size, copies each non-deleted clause, rebuilds clauses and by_tier (which also removes all stale tier entries), and for marked clauses rewrites the implication graph's reason to the new ref.

This is the reason ClauseRef can be a plain offset: the only long-lived holders are the database lists, the watch lists (rebuilt) and reasons (patched).

children.title: Decision heuristic (decision/)
children.summary: Which variable to branch on (VSIDS) and which value to try (phase saving).
children.body: decision.rs is the thin make_decision wrapper; decision/vsids.rs is the heuristic. Upstream's one-line wrappers (make_available, initialize_var, remove_var) were inlined at their call sites during absorption.

children.title: VSIDS heap
children.summary: Variable State Independent Decaying Sum: bump variables seen in conflicts, decay all geometrically, branch on the max via an indexed binary heap.
children.body:
VSIDS (from Chaff, as refined in MiniSat) focuses search on variables involved in recent conflicts. Every variable met during conflict analysis (in the conflict clause or resolved on) gets bump added to its activity. After each conflict all activities decay by vsids_decay = 0.95. Decisions pick the highest-activity unassigned variable. This is VSIDS, not VMTF; the crate has no VMTF queue.

Implementation: rather than multiplying every activity by 0.95, decay() multiplies the bump by 1/0.95, so newer bumps simply weigh more. When anything passes f32::MAX / 16, rescale scales all activities and the bump down together. Activities are plain f32 (upstream's ordered-float was dropped; activities are never NaN).

The heap is a hand-written binary max-heap heap: Vec<Var> with a position: Vec<Option<usize>> index so bump and seed can sift_up in place. make_available inserts (called on backtrack), make_unavailable removes (called when a variable leaves the solver), and the Iterator impl pops the max. Assigned variables are lazily discarded at decision time rather than removed on assignment.

children.title: Phase saving
children.summary: A decided variable takes the value it had when last unassigned; never-assigned variables start false.
children.body:
After a backjump or restart, much of the abandoned assignment was fine. Phase saving makes the solver re-enter the same region by re-choosing each variable's previous value. backtrack records last_value[var] = (value == Some(true)) for every literal it pops, and make_decision uses decision_var.lit(assignment.last_var_value(var)).

The initial phase is false (the last_value vector is resized with false). In the planner's encoding most variables are "op o at layer t", so the default tries plans with no actions first and lets propagation from goals and frame axioms pull actions in. The 0.25 record notes this sparse-plan polarity came for free.

children.title: Conflict analysis
children.summary: analyze_conflict.rs: first-UIP learning, recursive minimization, and the backjump level.
children.body: Holds the reusable buffers in AnalyzeConflict (clause, current_level_count, var_flags, to_clean, involved, stack). conflict_step mem::takes the struct out after analysis so the learned clause can be read while the rest of the context is mutated.

children.title: 1UIP resolution walk
children.summary: Walk the trail newest-first, resolving away current-level literals until one remains; earlier-level literals go straight into the learned clause.
children.body:
add_literal is applied to every literal of the conflict and of each reason used. It skips level-0 literals (permanently false, so irrelevant) and duplicates (var_flags), bumps VSIDS, and then either counts the literal in current_level_count (current level) or pushes it into the output clause (earlier level).

The main loop scans trail().iter().rev(). For each flagged literal it decrements the count; if the count hits zero this literal is the first UIP, so !lit is pushed and swapped into position 0. Otherwise its reason's literals are added. Walking in reverse trail order guarantees each literal is resolved after everything it implied, which is what makes the cut unique.

Afterwards: minimize, clear flags via to_clean, find the highest-level remaining literal and swap it into position 1 so the clause's watches are correct after the backjump (position 1 must be the last literal to become unassigned), return its level, and call vsids.decay().

children.title: Recursive clause minimization
children.summary: Drop learned literals already implied by the others, found by DFS in the implication graph with a 64-bit Bloom filter of levels to prune.
children.body:
A learned literal is redundant if its negation is implied by the other literals of the clause: following reasons backwards from it, every path ends in literals already in the clause (or level 0). Removing such literals makes learned clauses shorter and stronger. This is MiniSat-style recursive minimization.

minimize_clause keeps position 0 and tests each other literal with lit_is_redundant, a DFS over reasons using analyze.stack. Two optimisations:

  • Level abstraction: LevelAbstraction is a 64-bit Bloom filter of the clause's decision levels (1 << (level % 64)). Reaching a literal whose level is definitely not in the clause, or a decision not in the clause, means the DFS would eventually hit an outside decision, so it aborts early.
  • Memoised success: var_flags doubles as the visited set. On failure the flags set during this DFS are rolled back; on success they stay, so later DFS runs treat those literals as known-implied and do not expand them.

children.title: Schedule
children.summary: schedule_step: budget check, Luby restart, periodic reductions, GC, one conflict_step, count++.
children.body: Schedule tracks conflicts (lifetime), next_restart, restarts, the LubySequence, and the ferroplan-added conflict_limit / conflicts_this_solve. schedule_step returns false when the state is decided or the budget is spent; otherwise performs any due restart, reduction and garbage collection, then exactly one conflict_step. Upstream's log telemetry was removed with the dependency.

children.title: Luby restart sequence
children.summary: Restart intervals follow 1,1,2,1,1,2,4,1,... times 128 conflicts: mostly short runs with occasional long ones.
children.body:
The Luby sequence (OEIS A182105) is the provably near-optimal universal schedule for restarting a randomised algorithm whose run-time distribution is unknown (Luby, Sinclair, Zuckerman 1993). It is "reluctant doubling": 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 4, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 4, 8, ... LubySequence::advance computes it in O(1) state with two u64s using Knuth's 2012 method (u & -u == v test).

schedule_step multiplies each term by luby_restart_interval_scale = 128, so restarts happen after 128, 128, 256, 128, 128, 256, 512, ... conflicts. A unit test pins the first 64 terms. There is no glucose-style dynamic restart policy.

children.title: Input and simplification
children.summary: How clauses get in (DIMACS, load_clause) and how permanent facts shrink the database.
children.body: The entry side of the solver: parsing, normalising and storing new clauses, plus the level-0 simplifier that keeps the stored formula small as facts are proven.

children.title: DIMACS reader / writer
children.summary: A ferroplan-original, dependency-free DIMACS CNF parser and writer replacing the unabsorbed varisat-dimacs crate.
children.body:
DIMACS CNF is the standard SAT interchange text format: c comment lines, a p cnf VARS CLAUSES header, and clauses as whitespace-separated signed integers terminated by 0. parse_dimacs(BufRead) accepts clauses that span or share lines, an optional header (duplicate or malformed headers are errors), and checks after reading that the variable count does not exceed the header and the clause count matches. Errors carry a 1-based line number (DimacsError::Parse { line, msg }) or wrap I/O.

parse_dimacs_str is the string convenience; write_dimacs emits p cnf plus one line per clause. Unit tests cover multi-line clauses, the empty clause, five error shapes and a round trip.

The planner does not go through DIMACS; it calls add_clause directly. DIMACS serves the satdiff battery and debugging dumps.

children.title: Clause loading
children.summary: load_clause: map to solver vars, sort, dedup, drop tautologies, drop satisfied, then dispatch to unit / binary / long storage.
children.body:
Every clause from the caller enters through load_clause. It returns immediately if the solver is already UNSAT, flips SAT back to Unknown, and does a full_restart (new clauses invalidate the current trail). Then:

  1. Map user literals to solver literals (allocating variables as needed); sort and dedup.
  2. Tautology check: after sorting, x and !x are adjacent (codes differ only in the low bit); a tautology is ignored.
  3. Clear isolated on every variable of a clause of length 2+.
  4. Against level-0 assignments: a true literal drops the clause; false literals are set aside and their units resurrected; unassigned literals are moved to the front so they will be the watched ones.
  5. Dispatch: empty is UNSAT; one literal is enqueued as a unit (or UNSAT if it was only false literals); two go to BinaryClauses; three or more go to db::add_clause with Tier::Irred.

children.title: Unit simplification
children.summary: Level-0 facts are moved off the trail, satisfied clauses deleted, false literals stripped, and fixed variables recycled.
children.body:
A literal assigned at decision level 0 is true in every model, permanently. prove_units (called after every propagate in find_conflict) detects level 0, marks each trail literal a removed unit in the implication graph (depth sentinel), and clears the trail. If any were new, unit_simplify runs:

  1. simplify_binary drops binary entries involving assigned literals.
  2. filter_clauses over long clauses: delete any with a true literal; strip false literals; a clause reduced to two literals becomes a binary clause; longer ones are rewritten in place with a smaller length. Empty or unit results are unreachable! after full propagation.
  3. For every solver variable: if assigned, record VarData::unit and mark isolated; if isolated and not assumed, remove_solver_var frees its slot.

resurrect_unit is the inverse: when a newly loaded clause contains a removed unit's false literal, the unit is put back on the trail with Reason::Unit so the new clause will be propagated and later simplified.

children.title: Where the planner uses it
children.summary: The SAT compilation wing in crates/ferroplan/src/sat.rs encodes bounded horizons into a fresh Solver and decodes models into plans.
children.body:
The only caller is ferroplan's SAT wing, crates/ferroplan/src/sat.rs (owned and described under mod-sat). Briefly, from this crate's side:

  • EncTask::encode(h) builds a fresh Solver per horizon h and emits clauses with Lit::from_index(v, bool) over its own variable layout (fact@layer, op@layer, disabling-chain accumulators): initial-state units, goal units, mutex binaries, precondition and effect clauses, frame axioms, and for temporal tasks token, pairing and interval-interference clauses. Many are binaries, which hit the cheap implication-list path. It then optionally calls seed_activity under FF_SAT_BRANCH.
  • solve_horizon solves in conflict-limited slices (SLICE = 4_096), with a conflict-rate bail against the wall clock. Ok(true): the model is decoded; for the temporal face an STN check can return refutation clauses, which are added with add_clause and the same solver re-solves (CEGAR, relying on incrementality). Ok(false): UNSAT at this horizon. Err: budget slice spent.
  • ramp tries horizons 1, 2, 4, ... and moves on after UNSAT or budget exhaustion; a budget trip is never reported as unsolvable.

Not used by the planner today: assume/failed_core and DIMACS. lib.rs notes the solver's API and internals are shaped by this one caller.
facts: new, add_clause, seed_activity, set_conflict_limit, solve, model

children.title: Provenance and gate
children.summary: Where the code came from and the test battery every change must pass.
children.body: Two facts frame the whole crate: it is a port of varisat that ferroplan now owns, and no change lands unless the satdiff differential battery still reproduces every verdict and validates every model.

children.title: Origins: absorbed from varisat
children.summary: Ported from varisat 0.2.2 by Jannis Harder in the 0.24 cycle, stripped to zero dependencies, and owned as ferroplan code since.
children.body:
ferroplan-sat is not a dependency on a SAT library. In the 0.24 cycle the solver core of varisat 0.2.2 (Jannis Harder, github.com/jix/varisat, master @ 33e876937c5d, crates varisat and varisat-formula) was copied into the tree and carried forward as ferroplan's own code. The license is MIT OR Apache-2.0, identical to ferroplan's, so it carries through unchanged. Every absorbed file opens with a header naming its upstream path and what was changed.

Why absorb instead of depend: the 0.24 costing read found no pure-Rust solver better than MiniSat-class, vendoring only saved calendar time, and owning the code unlocks planning-specific branching (Madagascar's bespoke CDCL beat generic solvers on planning CNFs). The owner's instruction was "I want it to become our code, and us carry it forward."

What was stripped: proof logging (DRAT/LRAT), the self-checker, sampling-mode/witness variables, the partial_ref context-borrow macros, and the dependencies partial_ref, vec_mut_scan, ordered-float, rustc-hash, log, serde. Not absorbed: varisat-dimacs (replaced by a small original dimacs.rs), varisat-checker, varisat-lrat, varisat-cli and the internal proof/macro crates. Result: 5,012 lines kept from upstream's 7,414, zero external dependencies (dev-deps included). Added: one thing only, a per-solve conflict budget. The upstream checkout is kept at .solver-refs/varisat (gitignored) for differential comparison.

children.title: satdiff differential battery
children.summary: The test gate built before the absorption: fixture CNFs with known verdicts, every SAT model checked by direct clause evaluation.
children.body:
The crate's only referee is tests/satdiff.rs. It was written before the absorption (ferroplan's fixtures-first rule) and went red against a deliberately lying always-UNSAT stub before it ever went green against the real core. It then re-greened after every strip commit.

  • Small fixtures: tests/satdiff/*.cnf (22 files: pigeonhole php-*, graph colouring color-*, XOR pair, chains, and planning-shaped layered chains such as plan-chain-t3.cnf and plan-chain-slack.cnf). Each carries a c expect: SAT|UNSAT header and optionally c unique-model:. The loader asserts at least 15 exist.
  • Model check: verify_model evaluates every clause against the returned model; the solver never grades itself.
  • Mediums: three deterministic ~100k-clause instances generated in code (chain UNSAT, planted 3-SAT, layered chain). The 0.24 record notes they decide in 8-38 ms.
  • API behaviour: assumptions plus failed core on a conditional pigeonhole, incremental clause adding (verdict may only flip SAT to UNSAT, exactly once), conflict-budget interrupt then resume, and DIMACS naming of Var.
